zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Supplied page subset used for entry identification, not as authority for this copy’s typography or spelling. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Transcription corrections and English notes are independently based on the supplied BnF scans.

runs.text: O brincar, ou bulir dagoa com

lines.note: Mizzunaburi denotes playing with or stirring water; the Portuguese action is completed by the reference to the hand in the following physical line. The page begins by completing the preceding leaf’s Mizzu- catchword.
The short continuation specifies doing this with the hand. Preserve the printed contraction amão rather than introducing a modern word boundary.
Mizzunaxi is a separate pear entry, glossed as certain juicy pears, not a continuation of water-play. Its M is at the normal headword margin, so the provisional indentation is removed.

runs.text: Coco pera beber agoa no caminho.

lines.note: Mizzunomi names a drinking vessel for use on a journey, here called a coco in Portuguese. The damaged g of agoa remains identifiable; preserve the printed historical spelling without inserting a d from adjacent dagoa phrases.
The poetic expression Mizzuno vomo is equated with Mizzuno vomote. The Portuguese explanation follows on the next line; P. remains the printed usage label rather than part of the Japanese expression.
The gloss identifies the expression as the surface of water. Preserve Superficie and the joined dagoa as printed.

These are the paired calendrical names Mizzunoye and Mizzunoto. Enlarged reinspection shows a long descending stroke and faint upper residue between o and e, unlike the clear comma after e: read a damaged y, not the OCR comma and a separate e. The supplied NINJAL entry supports identification but does not replace the scan. The y remains the least securely preserved letter of this chosen reading; v- continues as vſão below.

runs.text: ſão os que contão os dias, & annos ſegundo o

lines.note: The explanation says these terms are used by people who count days and years according to the system named next. The tilde-bearing forms and the doubled n of annos are historical print, not errors.
This completes the reference to the Japanese calendrical repertory. Iapão is the Portuguese country name with consonantal I, not a Japanese headword.

runs.text: Vaſo deter agoa no Chanoyu, pe-

lines.note: Mizzuſaxi is a water container used in Chanoyu. The Japanese tea-practice term is embedded in the Portuguese sentence, and pe- continues as pera in the next line; retain the joined deter.

runs.text: ra ceuar a que esta na panella de ferro ao fogo.

lines.note: The vessel supplies or replenishes water already in an iron pot over the fire. Ceuar expresses this replenishing function; there is no reason to modernize the printed spelling or to treat this as another entry.

runs.text: Burbulhas, ou eſpelhos que ſe a-

lines.note: Mizzutama denotes bubbles or mirror-like appearances rising on water. Preserve the Portuguese alternatives Burbulhas and eſpelhos and the a- / leuantão division rather than substituting a modern technical term.
The Portuguese finishes the image of bubbles rising in water, then the Japanese example Mizzutamaga chi- begins. The final hyphen belongs to the interrupted verb chiru, not to the noun.

runs.text: Eſpalhar em ſe estas burbulhas dagoa.

lines.note: The continuation ru completes chiru; the gloss describes these bubbles scattering. The line belongs to Mizzutama, and the historical reflexive wording is retained instead of rewriting it as modern Portuguese.
Mizzutame is a reservoir or impounded water. The visible breve-like flourish in the italic initial of Repreſa is typography, not a Japanese reading mark.
Mizzutana, alternatively faxiri, is a board on which things are washed. The upright l introduces the alternative name; this is not a new Portuguese word or a citation.

runs.text: a louſa, ou outra couſa nacozinha.

lines.note: The objects washed are dishes or other things in the kitchen. Keep the old louſa and the joined nacozinha; this short continuation is not an independent headword.

runs.text: Gumil, ou jarro com que bo-

lines.note: The headword begins Mizzutçugui, not OCR Nizzutçugui: the scan has the same capital M as adjacent water compounds. The gloss names a pouring jug or ewer, with bo- continuing in botão.
This completes botão agoa, explaining that the jug is used to pour water. The tilde and historical agoa are retained rather than modernized.
This first Mizzutçuqi means a syringe-like water squirt. Cami is the regional label embedded in the Portuguese comparison, not a second headword on this row.
The line supplies Mizzufajiqi as the name used in Cami. Preserve the visible f and j in the Japanese spelling; the term is introduced within the Portuguese regional explanation.

runs.text: Ferros do freo que ſaem fora da

lines.note: The repeated Mizzutçuqi is a distinct entry for metal parts of a bridle bit protruding from the mouth. Freo is the historical Portuguese form, not a cue to combine this sense with the water-squirt entry.

runs.text: boca do caualo dambas as partes.

lines.note: Correct hoca to boca: the scan has b and the gloss describes the horse’s mouth on both sides. Preserve the contraction dambas.
Mizzutori is a water bird, with marreca and the divided la- / uanco as examples. Preserve the printed Paßaro and do not identify a single modern species from this generic definition.
The fragment uanco completes lauanco, a water-bird example begun on the previous row. The concluding &c. leaves the list open rather than introducing another term.
Mizzuvmi is glossed as lake or lagoon. Preserve the Japanese v used for a vowel in this position and the historical Portuguese lagoa.
Mizzuvochi denotes the pit or mouth of the stomach. The print reads eſtamago rather than the modern Portuguese form; neither the anatomical gloss nor the headword should be silently regularized.
Mizzuxino tana names cupboards or shelves. The following rows specify their contents; retain the printed separation before tana and the old Portuguese Almarios and partileiros.

runs.text: em que metem peças do Chanoyu, ou outras

lines.note: Correct OCR nietem to metem: the printed italic m begins the verb meaning put. The cupboards hold Chanoyu utensils or other objects; Chanoyu is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

This final couſas completes the description of stored objects and closes the Mizzu sequence before the internal M ANTES DO O heading. It is a genuine short body row, unlike the duplicate detection beside the initial below.

The new section begins MO., with the large M extending beside the next physical row. The gloss marks the item as an adverb meaning already or enough. The spurious c1-l032 reused parts of this same M and basta; its fragments are absorbed here, with no independent printed row or text discarded.
This distinct Mo is the additive particle, glossed Tambem. The text says it is postposed; preserve the joined Sempreſe, and retain the visible indentation beside the enlarged initial above.
The grammatical explanation specifies nouns and verbal participles as hosts for the particle. The ampersand and &c. are retained; this is a continuation of Mo, not another entry.
Yorumo firumo illustrates the particle with night and day. The Portuguese expresses the pair in the opposite order, day and night; the line-ending noi- continues below.
The fragment te completes noite, followed by Netemo, voqitemo, asleep or awake. Preserve the comma between the paired Japanese forms and the interrupted Portuguese Dormin-.

runs.text: do, & eſperto. i, Sempre. ¶ Item, Com

lines.note: The gloss completes sleeping and waking and interprets their combination as always. A paragraph then introduces the particle’s behavior with negative verbs; the two functions should not be collapsed into a single English equivalent.

runs.text: verbos negativos tem força denegar. Vt,

lines.note: The print reads negativos and denegar, not the OCR splits nega tiuos and demegar. Here denegar represents the closely set words for negating in the Portuguese explanation. Yu- starts the Japanese example completed below.
Yumenimo zonjenu means not knowing it even in dreams, as the Portuguese Nem por ſonhos o ſei explains. The row is visibly inset like the other continuations, so its indentation is restored.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Ainda que, ou poſto que. Vt,

lines.note: Correct Autida to Ainda in the concessive gloss, although or even though. The Japanese example begins Ma- and continues with itemo below; retain the printed line division.
The fragment itemo completes Maitemo, with the gloss although I go or come. The grave accent in và is visible, and the physical line is indented rather than a new margin-aligned entry.
This separate Mo denotes sea growth or seaweed, described as certain limos of the sea. The headword has no added length mark; preserve domar as printed rather than imposing modern word spacing.
Mǒacu means great wickedness or sin. The caron over the Japanese vowel is distinct from the unaccented Mo above; the usage example follows in the next row.
Mǒacuuo xeiſuru is glossed as prohibiting or preventing great sins. The printed x and long ſ are retained in the verb; this example is an indented continuation of the preceding entry.
The Portuguese completes impedir sins, then Mǒacu butǒna introduces a description of an unrestrainedly wicked person. Preserve both carons and the visible sentence division.
Correct deſaſonado to deſaforado: the print has f and r, and the gloss describes a person excessive or unrestrained in sins and wickedness. The line ends in the divided mal-.
The fragment dades completes maldades and closes the first column. The lower rule is present in the crop, confirming that this is the complete final body row rather than a clipped continuation.
Mǒacujin is paraphrased as Mǒacuna fito, a wicked person. The separator after i is a comma in the scan; preserve the two visible carons and the per- / uerſo division in the Portuguese.
The continuation completes peruerſo and adds desalmado, giving morally perverse or heartless. This explains the human noun above rather than a new abstract sense of Mǒacu.

Mǒca is identified with Xiguat and the fourth Japanese lunar month. Enlarged second-pass inspection resolves the two upward outer strokes over o as a caron, correcting the first-pass circumflex. Preserve the printed final t of Xiguat instead of expanding the Japanese form.

runs.text: Pauiola, ou cesto com que acarretão

lines.note: Mocco names a carrying litter or basket. The Portuguese Pauiola is historical and is retained; the objects carried follow on the next row.
This completes the carrying-container definition: earth or another material. The phrase outra couſa should not be narrowed to a modern construction tool beyond what the gloss states.
This first Moccǒ is simply described as a certain medicine. The scan supplies no botanical identification, so the generic Portuguese mezinha is preserved without conjectural expansion.

runs.text: Certa marca, ou diuiſa, que abrem,

lines.note: The second Moccǒ denotes a mark or emblem engraved, impressed, or painted. It is a separate homonymous entry; retain the caron and the Portuguese diuiſa.

runs.text: ou imprimem em metal, ou que pintão nos

lines.note: The emblem may be impressed in metal or painted on the items listed next. This continuation distinguishes techniques and surfaces, not another Japanese term.
Correct Iação to Iapão: the printed descending letter is p. The examples are garments and Japanese hanging cloths; preserve the historical joined darmar.
Mochi here means birdlime, with Torimochi presented as the preferable form. Meliùs is italic editorial Latin; the following Mo- begins an example, not the rice-cake sense in the later entry.
Mochiuo nuru and the alternative tçuquru describe applying the birdlime. The printed l introduces the alternative verb; the Portuguese specifies application to a pole in the next row.
The birdlime is put on a pole or similar object to catch birds. Preserve paßaros and the explicit purpose clause, which confirms that the preceding mochi is adhesive rather than food.
This Mochi denotes round cakes made of rice, in contrast to the preceding birdlime entry. Preserve the joined darroz and do not add a preparation method absent from the gloss.
The verb entry Mochi, tçu, otta means to have, hold, or carry. The principal parts belong to the historical verb corresponding to motçu; they are not three independent words.
The gloss specifies carrying in the hands and possessing, then introduces Youo motçu. The printed ß in poßuir and the word division Youo motçu are preserved.

runs.text: Ter o gouerno, ou poßuir o reino. ¶

lines.note: Youo motçu is explained as holding the government or possessing a kingdom. A new example starts with Yacu and is completed by the following row’s alternative daiquan.
Yacu, alternatively daiquanuo motçu, concerns holding an office or delegated position. The gloss and the l alternative marker show why the row continues the example above.

runs.text: ou estar em lugar doutro como feitor, gouer-

lines.note: The explanation includes standing in another person’s place as an agent or governor. Preserve doutro and the gover- division, without forcing a modern Japanese administrative title onto the example.
The fragment nador completes gouernador and closes the office-holding example. The final &c. remains part of the Portuguese gloss.
Correct Fita- to Fiza-: the visible z and the following Portuguese joelhos identify knees. Mochiague means to lift up, and the example continues with uo mochiaguru on the next line.
The phrase Fizauo mochiaguru is glossed as raising the knees. The row’s initial uo is the continuation after the line-end Fiza-, not a new headword.
Mochiai means to happen to have something. Both principal-part vowels carry carons in the scan; the Portuguese cou- continues as couſa below.

Mochiyǒtaniyotte xinzuru gives an example of offering something because one happened to have it. Preserve the printed sequence Mochiyǒtaniyotte without inferred Japanese morpheme spaces. At the right rule Por has no trailing hyphen: enlarged second-pass inspection shows clean blank paper after r, so the OCR hyphen is removed while quanto remains on the next row.

runs.text: quanto acertei deter iſto volo offereço, ou dou.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the reason for giving or offering the object. Retain deter, iſto, volo, and offereço as historical spellings and spacing rather than rewriting the sentence in modern Portuguese.

Mochiaraxi describes allowing a possession to deteriorate. The scan supports the unusual principal-part punctuation ſu aita without an added comma; the Portuguese has em velhe at the line end, with no hyphen supplied editorially.

runs.text: cendo, & danando a caſa, ou caualo, &c.

lines.note: The continuation cendo completes the aging expression and adds damaging a house, horse, or similar possession. Preserve the historical danando and the cross-line wording rather than joining it into a modernized sentence.

The Japanese example names either a house or a horse as the object of mochi araſu. The printed space in mochi araſu and the alternative marker l are retained; they are not normalized to the headword’s single-word spelling.
Mochiatçucai first means handling or manipulating something. The caron-bearing principal parts are distinct from the plain vowels elsewhere on the page.

runs.text: algũa couſa com as mãos. ¶ Item, Enfa-

lines.note: The first gloss specifies handling with the hands, then a paragraph begins the further sense of becoming frustrated. Enfa- is a Portuguese word division continued by darſe below.

runs.text: darſe de algũa couſa que hum tratou, & não

lines.note: The extended sense concerns frustration with a matter one has dealt with but cannot remedy. The tilde in algũa and the negation não are retained in the printed sentence.

The phrase about not finding a remedy completes the second sense, followed by Cono coto-. The inherited spacing a cha is retained because the type is visibly loose here; context identifies the verb achar without licensing silent normalization.
Cono cotouo mochiatçucǒta illustrates being at a loss or tired of the matter. Retain the caron in the past form and the joined Eſtouja in its Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: iſto, ou não lhe acho remedio, &c.

lines.note: The Portuguese finishes the example: being fed up with this, or unable to find a remedy. This is a continuation of the preceding sentence, not an independent meaning attached to the next headword.
Mochiauaxe means to happen to have something. Preserve the historical paradigm ſuru, eta rather than substituting uru on the basis of a modern verb; the longer cited example begins below.
The example begins with a speaker saying that this was something he himself happened to have. Mizzucaraga is the self-reference expression, not another water compound; the line ends in at- before te.

The sentence continues with thirty bolts of rolled silk and the recipient named Muſaxi. Preserve ſanjippiqi and the split ma- / yeni, and do not replace the Japanese proper name with the Portuguese gloss’s alternative name.
The quotation continues that the silk was piled before the recipient. Yax. is the printed citation label and remains roman, followed by the italic Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: iſto a certara de ter, pos diante de Benquei 30.

lines.note: Correct OCR go. to the visible numeral 30. The Portuguese says the speaker put thirty pieces before Benquei, agreeing with ſanjippiqi in the Japanese; retain the separate printed a certara rather than silently modernizing the spacing.
This completes the description as pieces of Japanese silk. The Portuguese translation names the recipient differently from the Japanese quotation, which is preserved rather than harmonized.

Correct Mochidacnu to Mochidachi, a large sword carried behind someone, as Montante explains. Enlarged second-pass comparison with the following headword shows an exceptional slanted italic initial M followed by roman ochidachi; preserve that mixed type rather than italicizing the whole Japanese word. The damaged inner strokes of dachi are read from the remaining letterforms and the lexical context.
Mochi facobi means to carry or transport. The scan supports the separated headword and the caron in ǒda; retain these instead of regularizing them to another occurrence’s paradigm.
The short continuation supplies the object, some thing, and closes the carrying definition. It is visibly indented in the scan, so the missing placement marker is restored.

runs.text: Arroz de que ſe fazẽ Mochis.

lines.note: Mochigome is rice from which Mochis are made. Mochis is a Japanese loan embedded in the Portuguese explanation and retains the visible capital and plural s.
Mochiguſocu denotes weapons such as a lance or partisan. The long ſ in the Japanese word and the divided Portuguese parta- are retained.
The fragment ſana completes partaſana, followed by &c. This is an indented continuation of the weapons entry, not a headword.
Mochij, iru, ita is glossed as esteeming or valuing. The example starts with Mochijru; preserve the historical ij spelling rather than replacing it with a modern normalized form.

The example says that when valued or employed even a mouse becomes a tiger. Its contrast begins mochij- at the row end; the separate far-right zaru below is the catchword, not an extra body row, so it is retained as page furniture. The continuation is visibly inset from the headword margin, and its missing indentation marker is restored.
